topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: What is the difference between a fiscal deficit and the national debt?
options: A deficit is a flow in one period; the debt is the accumulated stock
A deficit is the stock; the debt is the flow
A deficit applies to central government and the debt to local government
They are the same thing
questions.why: A deficit of $40bn this year adds $40bn to the debt.
whyNot: The definitions are the other way round.
Both usually refer to the whole public sector.
One is annual borrowing, the other cumulative.

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: The deficit falls from $60bn to $40bn. What happens to the debt?
options: It rises by $40bn
It falls by $20bn
It is unchanged
It falls by $40bn
questions.why: Government borrowing is falling and total debt is still growing. The debt only falls if there is a surplus.
whyNot: A smaller deficit still adds to the debt.
Any deficit adds to the debt.
That would require a surplus.

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: Which of the following best defines an automatic stabiliser?
options: A feature of the tax and benefit system that moderates the cycle without any deliberate decision
A deliberate change in tax rates to influence the economy
A central bank rule for setting interest rates
A limit on the size of the fiscal deficit
questions.why: In a recession revenue falls and benefit spending rises, both supporting demand and widening the deficit automatically.
whyNot: That is discretionary fiscal policy.
That is a monetary policy rule.
That is a fiscal rule.

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a structural deficit?
options: The part of a deficit that would remain even at trend output
The part of a deficit caused by the economy running below trend
A deficit caused by a one-off event such as a pandemic
A deficit funded by borrowing from abroad
questions.why: It reflects a permanent gap between committed spending and what the tax system raises, so it will not disappear with recovery.
whyNot: That is the cyclical deficit.
That is a temporary shock.
The funding source does not define it.

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: A deficit is $40bn and GDP is $800bn. What is the deficit as a share of GDP?
questions.why: (40 / 800) x 100 = 5.0%. Both the deficit and the debt should always be expressed as a share of GDP.
whyNot: That uses an incorrect calculation.
That inverts part of the calculation.
That misplaces the decimal point.

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: Why does a cyclical deficit require no corrective action?
options: It disappears automatically as the economy recovers, and tightening would deepen the recession
It is too small to matter
It is not counted in the national debt
It is funded by the central bank
questions.why: Tightening to close it reduces revenue further and may not reduce the deficit at all, which is the central criticism of austerity in a downturn.
whyNot: It can be very large in a deep recession.
It adds to the debt like any other borrowing.
Funding does not determine the classification.

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: What is the practical difficulty with the cyclical and structural distinction?
options: Trend output is not observable, and estimates of it are revised substantially
Neither concept has a definition
Governments are not allowed to publish the split
The two are identical in practice
questions.why: So the policy conclusion rests on an estimate nobody can verify at the time, which is an excellent evaluation point.
whyNot: Both are precisely defined.
Estimates are routinely published.
They behave very differently.

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: How can a debt-to-GDP ratio fall while the debt itself rises?
options: If GDP grows faster than the debt
If the deficit rises faster than GDP
If interest rates rise
Only if the government runs a surplus
questions.why: Historically this is how most large debt ratios have fallen, through growth and inflation rather than surpluses.
whyNot: That would raise the ratio.
Higher rates raise debt servicing and the deficit.
A surplus is not required if growth is fast enough.

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: What is the main limitation of automatic stabilisers?
options: They only moderate the cycle and do not correct a deep recession
They act too slowly to be useful
They require a decision each time
They are unavailable in developed economies
questions.why: They are also weaker where the tax system is less progressive and benefits less generous, which is typical of developing economies.
whyNot: Their advantage is that they act immediately.
They operate without any decision.
They are strongest in developed economies.

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: Which condition determines whether a debt ratio is on a rising or falling path?
options: Whether nominal GDP grows faster than the interest rate on the debt
Whether the deficit is above or below 3% of GDP
Whether the debt is held domestically or abroad
Whether the government runs a primary surplus
questions.why: If growth exceeds the interest rate, the ratio falls even with a deficit. This is the technical heart of debt sustainability.
whyNot: Fixed thresholds are policy conventions, not economic conditions.
That affects the risk, not the arithmetic of the path.
A primary surplus helps, and the growth-interest comparison is the general condition.

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: Why is the three lags problem a limitation of discretionary fiscal policy?
options: Recognition, decision and implementation lags mean the measure may take effect after the recession has ended
Discretionary policy cannot be targeted
Discretionary policy is prohibited during a recession
Discretionary policy has no multiplier effect
questions.why: A stimulus arriving after recovery adds to inflation instead of supporting output.
whyNot: Its advantage is that it can be large and targeted.
It is the standard response to a recession.
It has a multiplier effect; the issue is timing.

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: Why is foreign currency debt more dangerous than domestic currency debt?
options: A depreciation raises the real burden of servicing it, often when export earnings have fallen
Foreign currency debt carries no interest
It cannot be rescheduled
It is not counted in the national debt
questions.why: This is a serious vulnerability for developing economies and connects to the foreign currency gap.
whyNot: It carries interest like any debt.
It can be rescheduled, as debt relief programmes show.
It is counted.

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: Why have several high-debt countries borrowed at historically low rates?
options: The relationship between borrowing and interest rates depends on capacity, the central bank and confidence
High debt always lowers interest rates
Interest rates are set by the WTO
Investors do not observe debt levels
questions.why: Rates rise when markets doubt the debt is sustainable, and that judgement is partly self-fulfilling rather than mechanical.
whyNot: There is no such automatic relationship.
The WTO does not set interest rates.
Investors watch them closely.

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: Why is debt servicing described as an opportunity cost?
options: Money spent on interest cannot fund health, education or infrastructure
Interest payments are not a real cost
Debt servicing raises the exchange rate
Interest is paid only in a surplus year
questions.why: It is the first claim on tax revenue, and for developing economies it can consume a very large share of export earnings.
whyNot: They are a substantial real cost.
There is no such automatic effect.
Interest is contractual and due every year.

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: Which argument suggests debt is less of a burden on future generations than it appears?
options: Debt is mostly owed by a government to its own citizens, so it is partly an internal transfer
Future generations will have no taxes to pay
Debt is written off automatically after a fixed period
Interest payments are not made to anyone
questions.why: Future generations are also typically richer, and failing to invest now imposes a cost on them too.
whyNot: They will service the debt through taxation.
Debt is repaid or refinanced, not automatically written off.
Interest is paid to bondholders.

questions.topicTitle: Public sector borrowing and public sector debt
questions.stem: Which factor is the principal source of structural fiscal pressure in most developed economies?
options: An ageing population raising pension, health and social care spending
Falling debt interest costs
A growing informal economy
Rising commodity prices
questions.why: The working population funding those commitments shrinks at the same time, which is what makes the pressure structural.
whyNot: Interest costs rise with debt.
That is more significant in developing economies.
That affects commodity importers cyclically.
